sources.source_report_limitations: This is a macaque anatomo-functional connectivity study, not a seizure study. The behavioral observations derive from ICMS maps, including maps from prior work, and the stimulation used a 4 mA, 50 Hz, 3-second train after a quiet baseline; the authors note that insular responses may recruit large-scale networks beyond the stimulated site. The paper contains no patients with insular seizures, no spontaneous ictal or postictal observations, no seizure-onset reference standard, and no patient or seizure denominators for the stimulation-evoked behaviors. Resting-state fMRI was acquired in sedated macaques, and tract-tracing and connectivity results provide network context rather than direct evidence of seizure expression. Bibliographic citations to human insular stimulation or seizure studies do not convert this source into a seizure study.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The paper summarizes prior macaque ICMS mapping performed with 200-microsecond biphasic pulses at 50 Hz, 4 mA, for 3 seconds; a behavior entered the dataset when two observers recognized it and it was evoked in more than 50% of trials. The present analyses used ICMS maps and insular tracer injections in two male rhesus macaques (Mk1 and Mk2), indirect tracer data from 22 additional animals, and resting-state fMRI from 12 male macaques aged 4-8 years. The authors warped the ICMS maps and injection sites onto the INIA19 macaque template and delineated six insular fields. No seizure cohort, ictal or postictal observations, or clinical localization reference standard was studied.
sources.source_report_summary: Simone et al., Progress in Neurobiology 247 (2025) 102748, is an original experimental nonhuman-primate study combining macaque intracortical microstimulation (ICMS)-defined insular field maps, tract tracing, and resting-state fMRI to characterize insular anatomo-functional networks. The functional-localization observations below are stimulation-evoked macaque behaviors; this source is not a seizure study.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a narrative review with heterogeneous cited populations and no single source cohort, unified ascertainment method, quantitative evidence table, or source-verified cited-study dataset. The review mentions that FCD may have “particular ictal changes” on EEG and that lissencephaly may have a characteristic interictal EEG appearance, but it does not name or describe those patterns; they are therefore not represented as sign-level findings. The bilateral perisylvian polymicrogyria phenotype, congenital hemiparesis, developmental delay, pseudobulbar palsy, and spastic quadruparesis are non-ictal developmental or neurological features and are not converted into seizure-atlas findings. No claim in this report establishes a body-side or hemisphere direction.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The article is a narrative review rather than a single primary cohort. The review states that it identified material through MEDLINE and Current Contents searches using MCD, malformation, epilepsy, named-gene, and related terms, supplemented by relevant articles and the author's files; only papers published in English were reviewed. The populations and designs vary across the cited reports and are often not specified in the review text. Cohort descriptors, prevalence estimates, surgery outcomes, treatment response, mortality, and developmental context are retained only as background when needed to interpret an in-scope claim, not as independent atlas findings.
sources.source_report_summary: This is a narrative clinical review by Sanjay M Sisodiya, published as Malformations of cortical development: burdens and insights from important causes of human epilepsy (Lancet Neurol 2004;3:29-38). It surveys focal cortical dysplasia, periventricular heterotopia, polymicrogyria, subcortical band heterotopia and lissencephaly, dysembryoplastic neuroepithelial tumours, and microdysgenesis. This report retains only source-reported seizure manifestations or statements that bear directly on epileptogenic localization; malformation taxonomy, genetics, imaging descriptors, treatment, outcomes, and general burden are not represented as findings.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a single case report with no comparator, reference standard, cohort-level denominator, statistical analysis, or uncertainty estimates. Initial ictal scalp EEG was nonlocalizable, while MRI and FDG-PET did not identify a focal abnormality. The authors note that the first resection could have affected the brain network and that more cases are needed; cited-study statements above were not independently reviewed.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Single case report: an 18-year-old right-handed girl with medically refractory reflex and spontaneous seizures since age 12. The evaluation included MRI, FDG-PET, scalp and long-term video EEG, two MEG analyses, two chronic subdural-electrode evaluations with functional mapping, ictal SPECT during provocation, resections, histopathology, and postoperative follow-up. No comparator or reference standard was reported.
sources.source_report_summary: Suzuki et al., “The Involvement of Sensory-motor Networks in Reflex Seizure,” NMC Case Report Journal 2017;4:127–130, is a single-patient case report describing stimulus-triggered reflex seizures, multimodal presurgical localization, two invasive evaluations and resections, ictal SPECT, and follow-up. The source is relevant to seizure semiology and case-specific left-sided and bilateral sensory-motor network localization.

sources.source_report_limitations: All 25 native pages were represented and reviewed; no page was blocked. This is an educational chapter combining review synthesis, cited-study restatements, a selected representative table, and one clinical case rather than one defined cohort. Many cited results lack denominators, response counts, effect sizes, or uncertainty estimates in the chapter, and cited sources were not independently reviewed. The source itself notes variability of stimulation responses, possible distant or systemic effects, incomplete understanding of functional networks, and difficulty interpreting memory mapping at the individual level. Table 10.1 is explicitly a selected sample; its final executive-function cell is visibly truncated to “No dis” in the rendered source and was not used for an in-scope finding. The chapter does not establish spontaneous-seizure semiology frequencies, diagnostic accuracy, or equivalence between stimulation-induced responses and spontaneous seizures.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The source describes clinical SEEG functional mapping using stimulation of sampled contacts during patient-specific tasks and summarizes cited studies involving patients with epilepsy, plus selected non-SEEG and awake-mapping studies in Table 10.1. Cited-study populations, sampling frames, analysis units, and denominators are frequently not reported in this chapter. One source-described clinical example is a 17-year-old patient with left temporo-perisylvian epilepsy and MRI-negative imaging (Fig. 10.4). The source distinguishes stimulation-induced clinical/electrophysiological responses from spontaneous seizures and treats afterdischarges as interpretation context.
sources.source_report_summary: Educational Chapter 10, “Electrical Stimulation for Functional Mapping During SEEG Exploration,” by Agnès Trébuchon and Daniel L. Drane in The Fundamentals of Stereoelectroencephalography (2025). The chapter reviews SEEG stimulation mapping and selected representative stimulation studies, with emphasis on how induced functional effects can localize functional sub-units and how they should be interpreted alongside seizure electro-clinical data. It is not a single spontaneous-seizure cohort.

findings.claim: The review states that seizure semiology localizes the symptomatogenic zone, which either overlaps or is close to the epileptogenic zone, and that later symptoms are more likely to reflect ictal spread and may have lateralizing rather than localizing value.
findings.evidence_text: “Seizure semiology is a simple and cost effective tool that allows localization of the symptomatogenic zone which either overlaps or is in close proximity of the epileptogenic zone.”
findings.laterality_localization: Symptomatogenic-zone localization is related to, but is not stated to be identical with, epileptogenic-zone localization; later spread-related signs may lateralize side without localizing origin
findings.limitations: NONE
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract; PDF p.1, Introduction
findings.population: Medically refractory focal epilepsy and epilepsy-surgery context; no single cohort reported

findings.claim: The review says an ideally useful localizing sign is easy to identify with high inter-rater reliability, occurs as the first or an early seizure component, and corresponds to a clearly defined and well-documented symptomatogenic zone; reproducibility with cortical stimulation identifies that zone, although not every ictal symptom is reproducible.
findings.evidence_text: “Ideally the signs used for localization should fulfill these criteria” followed by early timing, reliability, defined symptomatogenic zone, and stimulation-reproducibility criteria.
findings.laterality_localization: Localizing value is tied to a defined symptomatogenic zone; later components may have only lateralizing value
findings.limitations: NONE
findings.locators: PDF p.1, abstract
findings.phase: First or early ictal component emphasized
findings.population: Epilepsy-surgery evaluation; no single cohort reported
findings.source_term: criteria for signs used for localization

findings.citation: Reference 1: Syed TU, LaFrance WC Jr, Kahriman ES, Hasan SN, Rajasekaran V, Gulati D, et al. Can semiology predict psychogenic nonepileptic seizures? A prospective study. Ann Neurol 2011;69:997-1004.
findings.claim: The review reports that preserved awareness, eye flutter, and the ability of bystanders to modify or alleviate a typical event were significant markers of psychogenic non-epileptic events; normal alpha activity while the patient is unresponsive and amnestic for the event is described as essentially pathognomonic.
findings.evidence_text: “Preserved awareness, eye flutter and the ability of the bystanders to modify or alleviate were found to be significant markers”; normal alpha with unresponsiveness and amnesia is “essentially pathognomonic.”
findings.laterality_localization: NOT_APPLICABLE
findings.limitations: Cited-study restatement; the cited study was not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.1, Classification of Paroxysmal Events
findings.phase: During the typical paroxysmal event and post-event amnesia
findings.population: Typical psychogenic non-epileptic paroxysmal events; no cohort size reported in this review

findings.citation: References 2 and 3: Pugnaghi M, Meletti S, Castana L, Francione S, Nobili L, Mai R, et al. Features of somatosensory manifestations induced by intracranial electrical stimulations of the human insula. Clin Neurophysiol 2011;122:2049-2058; Stephani C, Fernandez-Baca Vaca G, Maciunas R, Koubeissi M, Luders HO. Functional neuroanatomy of the insular lobe. Brain Struct Funct 2011;216:137-149.
findings.claim: The review states that unilateral distal somatosensory auras confined to a clearly defined body region usually correspond to the contralateral primary sensory cortex, whereas bilateral or widespread sensations can arise from the supplementary sensorimotor area or S2; S2 stimulation can produce heat or pain, and poorly localized or lateralized “all body sensations” have no localizing or lateralizing value. Low-intensity motor-area stimulation may be perceived as a somatosensory aura when contractions do not produce actual movement.
findings.evidence_text: “The contralateral primary sensory cortex is usually the symptomatogenic zone” for unilateral distal auras; “Bilateral and more widespread” sensations can be produced from SSMA or S2; “all body sensations” have no localizing or lateralizing value.
findings.laterality_localization: Unilateral distal distribution points to contralateral primary sensory cortex; bilateral/widespread distribution can involve SSMA or S2; all-body sensations are explicitly nonlocalizing and nonlateralizing
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited stimulation literature; cited sources were not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.1, Somatosensory auras; PDF p.2, Somatosensory auras (continued)
findings.population: Patients with unilateral/distal, bilateral/widespread, or poorly localized somatosensory auras; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 4: Kuzniecky R. Symptomatic occipital lobe epilepsy. Epilepsia 1998;39 Suppl 4:S24-S31.
findings.claim: The review states that visual auras are often perceived in front of both eyes without clear lateralization, but may occasionally be lateralized to one visual field contralateral to the symptomatogenic zone and may be localized to an upper or lower field; simple visual hallucinations are assigned to Brodmann areas 17 and 18, while complex hallucinations or illusions more likely involve parieto-temporal association cortex or adjacent lobes. During or after amaurosis, flashing lights may appear over the blind field.
findings.evidence_text: Visual hallucinations are “frequently” reported in front of both eyes without clear lateralization; an aura may be lateralized to a visual field “contralateral to the symptomatogenic zone”; the symptomatogenic zone for visual hallucinations is Brodmann areas 17 and 18.
findings.laterality_localization: Bilateral visual reports are usually nonlateralizing; a unilateral visual field is contralateral to the symptomatogenic zone; simple versus complex visual phenomena are associated with primary versus association visual regions
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with one cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Visual auras
findings.phase: Aura; amaurosis may occur during or after the epileptic seizure
findings.population: Patients with visual auras; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 5: Florindo I, Bisulli F, Pittau F, Naldi I, Striano P, Striano S, et al. Lateralizing value of the auditory aura in partial seizures. Epilepsia 2006;47 Suppl 5:68-72.
findings.claim: The review describes simple auditory auras such as a buzz or noise as arising from Heschl's gyrus in the superior temporal gyrus and states that perceived sound laterality is not reliable for lateralizing the epilepsy, even when the patient perceives the sound on one side.
findings.evidence_text: “Even when the sound is perceived as lateralized to one side it is not a reliable sign to lateralize the epilepsy.”
findings.laterality_localization: Heschl's gyrus/superior temporal gyrus is the stated symptomatogenic zone; perceived sound side is not a reliable epilepsy-lateralizing direction
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Auditory auras
findings.population: Patients with simple auditory auras; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 6: Acharya V, Acharya J, Lüders H. Olfactory epileptic auras. Neurology 1998;51:56-61.
findings.claim: The review states that olfactory auras are usually unpleasant smells, have no lateralizing value, and are most frequently seen in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy; it also reports that a relatively high percentage of these patients have neoplasms involving the amygdala.
findings.evidence_text: “They have no lateralizing value but are most frequently seen in patients with mesial temporal lobe epilepsy”; a “relatively high percentage” have neoplasms involving the amygdala.
findings.laterality_localization: No lateralizing value; association with mesial temporal lobe and, in the review's cited statement, amygdala-involving neoplasms
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with an unquantified cited restatement
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Olfactory auras
findings.population: Patients with olfactory auras, particularly mesial temporal lobe epilepsy; percentage and cohort denominator not reported

findings.citation: Reference 3: Stephani C, Fernandez-Baca Vaca G, Maciunas R, Koubeissi M, Luders HO. Functional neuroanatomy of the insular lobe. Brain Struct Funct 2011;216:137-149.
findings.claim: The review describes gustatory auras as unpleasant tastes, states that cortical stimulation studies identify the insula as a symptomatogenic zone, and states that these auras have no lateralizing value.
findings.evidence_text: “Cortical stimulation studies have found the insula to be a symptomatogenic zone for this aura”; “These auras have no lateralizing value.”
findings.laterality_localization: Insular symptomatogenic zone; no lateralizing value
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Gustatory auras
findings.population: Patients with gustatory auras; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 7: Baumgartner C, Lurger S, Leutmezer F. Autonomic symptoms during epileptic seizures. Epileptic Disord 2001;3:103-116.
findings.claim: The review distinguishes subjective autonomic auras from “autonomic seizures,” which it says should be diagnosed when an autonomic alteration is objectively documented, such as tachycardia on ECG; the symptomatogenic zone of most autonomic auras is stated to be most likely the insular cortex.
findings.evidence_text: Autonomic seizures are described as having an autonomic alteration “that can be documented objectively”; the symptomatogenic zone of most autonomic auras is “most likely the insular cortex.”
findings.laterality_localization: Most autonomic auras are assigned most likely to the insular cortex; no laterality direction stated
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Autonomic auras; PDF p.3, Autonomic seizures
findings.population: Patients with autonomic auras or objectively documented autonomic seizures; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 8: Van Buren JM. The abdominal aura. A study of abdominal sensations occurring in epilepsy and produced by depth stimulation. Electroencephalogr Clin Neurophysiol 1963;15:1-19.
findings.claim: The review states that abdominal auras are frequent and usually secondary to temporal lobe epilepsy, but can occasionally be triggered by extratemporal epilepsy, mainly frontal or insular. The sensation usually begins in the epigastrium or midline stomach and may rise to the chest, throat, head, or face; when it rises to the neck or face, loss of consciousness is described as almost invariable. The review also reports that Van Buren's balloon studies found no gastromotor effect except rare gastric inhibition, and that stimulation has elicited similar sensations from the insula and other structures, with spread-related afterdischarges not excluded.
findings.evidence_text: “Abdominal auras are frequent and are usually secondary to temporal lobe epilepsies”; the sensation “begins usually in the epigastrium or stomach in the midline” and may rise to the neck or face, when the patient “loses consciousness.”
findings.laterality_localization: Usual temporal association with occasional frontal/insular extratemporal association; epigastric sensations can be elicited from insula, mesial temporal structures, basal ganglia, SSMA, pallidum, and centrum medianum of thalamus
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited stimulation findings and an explicit afterdischarge-spread qualification
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Abdominal auras
findings.phase: Aura; upward spread of the aura may precede loss of consciousness
findings.population: Patients with abdominal auras; cited spontaneous, induced, and stimulation observations, with no common cohort size reported

findings.citation: References 9 and 10: Devinsky O, Feldmann E, Burrowes K, Bromfield E. Autoscopic phenomena with seizures. Arch Neurol 1989;46:1080-1088; Bancaud J, Brunet-Bourgin F, Chauvel P, Halgren E. Anatomical origin of deja vu and vivid ‘memories’ in human temporal lobe epilepsy. Brain 1994;117:71-90.
findings.claim: The review states that psychic auras include complex hallucinations or illusions such as autoscopy, fear, elation, déjà vu, and jamais vu. The temporal lobe is usually involved in autoscopic phenomena, but they have no lateralizing value; stimulation has elicited related sensations from the temporal convexity or posterior temporal-occipital/parietal junction, with mesial temporal structures concurrently involved in most cited cases.
findings.evidence_text: “The temporal lobe is usually involved with these phenomena but they have no lateralizing value”; mesial temporal structures were “concurrently involved in most cases.”
findings.laterality_localization: Temporal and often mesial temporal involvement; no lateralizing value stated for autoscopic phenomena
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited stimulation and clinical reports; cited sources were not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.2, Psychic auras; PDF p.3, Psychic auras (continued)
findings.population: Patients with psychic or autoscopic auras; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 7: Baumgartner C, Lurger S, Leutmezer F. Autonomic symptoms during epileptic seizures. Epileptic Disord 2001;3:103-116.
findings.claim: The review states that pilomotor seizures have a somatotopic distribution and may spread in a Jacksonian-march-like pattern; they tend to be ipsilateral to the seizure-onset zone, but their localization value is poor.
findings.evidence_text: “Pilomotor seizures tend to be ipsilateral to the seizure onset zone, but the localization value is poor.”
findings.laterality_localization: Tends ipsilateral to seizure-onset zone; poor localization value
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Autonomic seizures
findings.population: Patients with pilomotor autonomic seizures; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 7: Baumgartner C, Lurger S, Leutmezer F. Autonomic symptoms during epileptic seizures. Epileptic Disord 2001;3:103-116.
findings.claim: The review states that ictal vomiting and retching are observed mainly in adult temporal lobe seizures, have no definite lateralizing value, and have some evidence supporting a role for the insula as visceral sensory cortex.
findings.evidence_text: “Ictal vomiting and ictal retching ... [are] observed mainly in temporal lobe seizures in adults. It has no definite lateralizing value.”
findings.laterality_localization: Mainly temporal lobe; no definite lateralizing value; possible insular visceral-sensory role
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Autonomic seizures
findings.population: Adults with temporal lobe seizures; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 11: Caboclo LO, Miyashira FS, Hamad AP, Lin K, Carrete H Jr, Sakamoto AC, et al. Ictal spitting in left temporal lobe epilepsy: report of three cases. Seizure 2006;15:462-467.
findings.claim: The review describes ictal spitting as a rare sign that also occurs in temporal lobe epilepsy and has no lateralizing value.
findings.evidence_text: “Ictal spitting is a rare sign that also occurs in temporal lobe epilepsy but has no lateralizing value.”
findings.laterality_localization: Temporal-lobe association; no lateralizing value
findings.limitations: Cited-study restatement; the cited cases were not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Autonomic seizures
findings.population: Patients with temporal lobe epilepsy; three-case report is identified in the cited reference, but no cohort is otherwise characterized in the review

findings.citation: Reference 12: Shah J, Zhai H, Fuerst D, Watson C. Hypersalivation in temporal lobe epilepsy. Epilepsia 2006;47:644-651.
findings.claim: The review states that ictal hypersalivation is an uncommon sign found more frequently in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy, particularly in the non-dominant hemisphere.
findings.evidence_text: “Ictal hypersalivation is another uncommon sign found more frequently in mesial temporal lobe epilepsy particularly in the non-dominant hemisphere.”
findings.laterality_localization: Mesial temporal association, with greater reported frequency in the non-dominant hemisphere
findings.limitations: Cited-study restatement; the cited study was not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Autonomic seizures
findings.population: Patients with mesial temporal lobe epilepsy; no cohort size reported

findings.citation: Reference 13: Wyllie E, Lüders H, Morris HH, Lesser RP, Dinner DS. The lateralizing significance of versive head and eye movements during epileptic seizures. Neurology 1986;36:606-611.
findings.claim: The review states that the epileptogenic zone in dialeptic seizures tends to be distant from primary or supplementary motor areas, whereas seizures originating at or near those areas tend to be predominantly motor and may have preserved consciousness; dialeptic seizures from mesial temporal structures are longer than those arising from the frontal lobe.
findings.evidence_text: “The duration ... has a localizing value with seizures originating from the mesial temporal structures being of longer duration than the ones arising from the frontal lobe.”
findings.laterality_localization: Dialeptic semiology is associated with distance from primary/SSMA motor areas; longer duration is associated with mesial temporal versus frontal origin
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Dialeptic seizures
findings.phase: Ictal consciousness alteration and seizure duration
findings.population: Patients with dialeptic seizures compared with seizures originating at or near primary or supplementary motor areas; no cohort reported

findings.citation: References 15 and 16: Bagla R, Skidmore CT. Frontal lobe seizures. Neurologist 2011;17:125-135; Werhahn KJ, Noachtar S, Arnold S, Pfänder M, Henkel A, Winkler PA, et al. Tonic seizures: their significance for lateralization and frequency in different focal epileptic syndromes. Epilepsia 2000;41:1153-1161.
findings.claim: The review states that focal tonic seizures preferentially affect proximal muscle groups, may be unilateral or bilateral, and tend to be asymmetric; consciousness is often preserved at onset. Preserved consciousness during bilateral motor activity can localize a focus to the supplementary motor area. Tonic seizures are reported in 62.2% of frontal-lobe epilepsy and 1.7% of temporal-lobe epilepsy; temporal-lobe tonic seizures were unilateral, whereas 32% of frontal-lobe tonic seizures were bilateral. A clearly unilateral tonic seizure has high lateralizing significance toward the contralateral seizure onset.
findings.evidence_text: “Tonic seizures occur most commonly in frontal lobe epilepsy (62.2%) and very rarely in temporal lobe epilepsy (1.7%).”
findings.laterality_localization: Bilateral motor activity with preserved consciousness can point to SSMA; clearly unilateral tonic activity points to contralateral seizure onset; temporal and frontal distributions differ as stated
findings.limitations: Review-reported comparative percentages; cited sources were not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.3, Tonic seizures
findings.population: Patients with focal epilepsy, compared between frontal-lobe and temporal-lobe epilepsy; cohort denominators not reported

findings.citation: Reference 17: Ohara S, Ikeda A, Kunieda T, Yazawa S, Taki J, Nagamine T, et al. Propagation of tonic posturing in supplementary motor area (SMA) seizures. Epilepsy Res 2004;62:179-187.
findings.claim: The review states that tonic seizures originating from the SSMA may appear bilateral from onset, but careful analysis can show initiation in one body part followed by rapid movement to other limbs; less often the posture is unilateral or restricted to one limb, while proximal-limb and axial involvement remains prominent.
findings.evidence_text: “Tonic seizures originating from the SSMA appear to be bilateral from the onset but careful analysis has revealed it may begin in one part of the body and move rapidly to the other limbs.”
findings.laterality_localization: SSMA-associated tonic posturing may look bilateral from onset but can have an initial focal body-part component; proximal and axial involvement is prominent
findings.limitations: Cited-study restatement; the cited study was not separately reviewed here

findings.citation: References 18, 19, and 20: Ajmone Marsan C, Ralston BL. The Epileptic Seizure, Its Functional Morphology and Diagnostic Significance: A Clinical-Electrographic Analysis of Metrazol-Induced Attacks. Springfield, IL: Charles C Thomas, 1957;85-88; Kotagal P, Bleasel A, Geller E, Kankirawatana P, Moorjani BI, Rybicki L. Lateralizing value of asymmetric tonic limb posturing observed in secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures. Epilepsia 2000;41:457-462; O’Brien TJ, Mosewich RK, Britton JW, Cascino GD, So EL. History and seizure semiology in distinguishing frontal lobe seizures and temporal lobe seizures. Epilepsy Res 2008;82:177-182.
findings.claim: The review describes a sequence beginning with version and tonic pulling of the face to the contralateral side, followed by the M2e fencing position and then asymmetric tonic limb posturing called the “sign of four.” It states that confidence in lateralizing the epileptogenic zone increases when at least two of the four signs are observed; the tonic face and versive signs point contralaterally, M2e points to the hemisphere contralateral to the raised arm, and the sign of four to the hemisphere contralateral to the extended arm. These signs lateralize but do not localize seizure origin.
findings.evidence_text: “The motor sequence includes 4 signs” and “the epileptogenic zone can be lateralized with confidence when 2 or more of these lateralizing signs are observed.”
findings.laterality_localization: Face tonic seizure and version contralateral; M2e contralateral to raised arm; sign of four contralateral to extended arm; signs lateralize but do not localize origin
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited sources; the review does not provide the underlying denominators or independent validation of the combination rule
findings.locators: PDF p.4, Tonic seizures
findings.phase: Ictal motor sequence before secondary generalization
findings.population: Patients with secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures; no cohort reported
findings.source_term: motor sequence in secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures

findings.citation: References 14, 21, and 22: Vendrame M, Zarowski M, Alexopoulos AV, Wyllie E, Kothare SV, Loddenkemper T. Localization of pediatric seizure semiology. Clin Neurophysiol 2011;122:1924-1928; Shields WD, Shewmon DA, Chugani HT, Peacock WJ. Treatment of infantile spasms: medical or surgical? Epilepsia 1992;33 Suppl 4:S26-S31; Juhász C, Chugani HT, Muzik O, Chugani DC. Neuroradiological assessment of brain structure and function and its implication in the pathogenesis of West syndrome. Brain Dev 2001;23:488-495.
findings.claim: The review describes epileptic spasms as relatively symmetric tonic or myoclonic contractions affecting proximal axial muscles, usually with trunk flexion and arm extension/abduction in a “salaam position”; they commonly occur in clusters as the patient goes to sleep and have predominantly generalized EEG patterns. They are usually seen with generalized epilepsies, but well-documented focal cases, particularly parieto-occipital, have undergone successful resective surgery; the mechanism is not clearly determined.
findings.evidence_text: “Usually epileptic spasms are seen in patients with generalized epilepsies. However, there are well documented cases ... particularly parieto-occipital epilepsies.”
findings.laterality_localization: Usually generalized epilepsy; focal cases particularly involving parieto-occipital regions are reported
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited pediatric and pathophysiology sources; cited sources were not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.4, Epileptic spasms
findings.phase: Ictal; often clustered at sleep onset
findings.population: Patients with generalized epilepsies and reported focal epilepsies, particularly parieto-occipital; no cohort reported

findings.citation: Reference 23: Janszky J, Fogarasi A, Jokeit H, Ebner A. Lateralizing value of unilateral motor and somatosensory manifestations in frontal lobe seizures. Epilepsy Res 2001;43:125-133.
findings.claim: The review states that clonic contractions recur at 0.2-5 per second and that the symptomatogenic zone is usually the primary motor strip. In temporal lobe epilepsy, the face, frontal eye field, and hand areas tend to be affected earlier than the legs; when clonus without altered consciousness is the first seizure sign, the epileptogenic zone is usually at or near the primary motor strip. Unilateral clonic seizures have high lateralizing value toward the contralateral hemisphere.
findings.evidence_text: “The symptomatogenic zone is usually the primary motor strip”; “Unilateral clonic seizures have a highly lateralizing value to the contralateral hemisphere.”
findings.laterality_localization: Primary motor strip; in temporal seizures face, frontal eye field, and hand earlier than legs; unilateral clonus contralateral
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited source; cited source was not separately reviewed here
findings.locators: PDF p.4, Clonic seizures
findings.phase: Ictal; first sign and early propagation emphasized
findings.population: Patients with focal epilepsy, including temporal lobe epilepsy; no cohort reported

findings.citation: References 24 and 25: Bonelli SB, Lurger S, Zimprich F, Stogmann E, Assem-Hilger E, Baumgartner C. Clinical seizure lateralization in frontal lobe epilepsy. Epilepsia 2007;48:517-523; Walser G, Unterberger I, Dobesberger J, Embacher N, Falkenstetter T, Larch J, et al. findings.claim: In secondarily generalized tonic-clonic seizures, the review states that clonic activity may persist longer on the side ipsilateral to the epileptogenic focus; it calls this “end of seizure paradoxical clonus” a highly reliable lateralizing sign and states that asymmetric seizure termination is relatively unusual in generalized epilepsy.

findings.claim: The review reserves the expression “tonic-clonic seizures” for generalized tonic-clonic seizures and states that onset with relatively symmetrical involvement of all limbs is highly suggestive of generalized epilepsy; focal epilepsies can also produce generalized tonic-clonic seizures, but these are almost always preceded by other seizure types and have a usually asymmetric tonic phase.
findings.evidence_text: “Occurrence of these types of seizures at the onset and relatively symmetrical involvement of all limbs is highly suggestive of generalized epilepsy.”

findings.claim: The review defines versive seizures as forced involuntary turning of the head and eyes in one direction with neck extension; the frontal eye fields are the symptomatogenic zone. Versive seizures appear earlier in frontal than temporal seizures and can be the first frontal-lobe sign; they have highly lateralizing value toward the contralateral hemisphere, especially within 10 seconds before secondary generalization. Reliability requires distinguishing epileptic versive seizures from non-versive natural head turning.
findings.evidence_text: “The frontal eye fields are the symptomatogenic zone”; versive seizures have “a highly lateralizing value to the contralateral hemisphere,” especially within 10 seconds before secondary generalization.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontal eye fields as symptomatogenic zone; earlier and sometimes first in frontal seizures; contralateral lateralization
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited sources and an explicit observer-interpretation qualification

findings.claim: The review describes hypermotor seizures as complex multijoint movements involving the trunk and proximal limbs, often occurring during sleep with possible preserved consciousness. Most are stated to originate from orbital or mesial frontal regions, although temporal and insular epilepsies can also produce them; some consist of sexual-activity-like automatisms with pelvic, limb, groin, or genital movements.

findings.claim: The review states that automotor seizures consist mainly of distal hand, foot, mouth, and tongue automatisms and are typical of temporal-lobe epilepsy, although they can occur in frontal-lobe seizures; frontal automotor seizures tend to be shorter. Unilateral automatisms are more frequently associated with an ipsilateral epileptogenic zone, possibly because contralateral limb dystonia interrupts distal automatisms. Altered consciousness accompanies 95% of automotor seizures, while preserved consciousness is observed almost exclusively in non-dominant mesial temporal epilepsy.
findings.evidence_text: “95% of the automotor seizures are associated with altered consciousness”; preservation of consciousness is observed “almost exclusively” in non-dominant mesial temporal epilepsy.

findings.citation: References 31 and 32: So NK. Atonic phenomena and partial seizures. A reappraisal. Adv Neurol 1995;67:29-39; Satow T, Ikeda A, Yamamoto J, Takayama M, Matsuhashi M, Ohara S, et al. Partial epilepsy manifesting atonic seizure: report of two cases. Epilepsia 2002;43:1425-1431.
findings.claim: The review states that atonic seizures occur most frequently in symptomatic generalized epilepsies, particularly Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and are usually preceded by a generalized proximal myoclonic seizure causing an abrupt fall and injury risk. Focal frontal- and temporal-lobe atonic seizures can occur but are usually not associated with myoclonus, producing slower falls that infrequently cause significant injury.
findings.evidence_text: “Atonic seizures are seen most frequently in patients with symptomatic generalized epilepsies (Lennox-Gastaut syndrome)” and can also occur in frontal and temporal focal epilepsies.
findings.laterality_localization: Generalized versus focal frontal/temporal association; no specific lateralizing direction
findings.limitations: Review synthesis with cited sources; cited sources were not separately reviewed here

findings.population: Symptomatic generalized epilepsy, especially Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, compared with focal frontal/temporal epilepsy

findings.claim: The review states that postictal aphasia lateralizes temporal-lobe epilepsy to the language-dominant hemisphere and that language recovery after the ictal EEG stops is significantly more delayed in left temporal lobe epilepsy. Postictal language delay is described as less affected in frontal-lobe epilepsy unless seizure activity extends to the ipsilateral temporal lobe. The review requires a cooperative patient who tries to understand and speak, continuous testing, and slow progressive recovery over 10-20 minutes.

sources.source_report_limitations: The source is a narrative review whose stated basis is a literature review plus results consistent with the authors' experience; it does not provide a reproducible search, eligibility process, unified cohort, common reference standard, or pooled estimate. Many cited results are restatements of other publications and are not primary findings of this document. Quantitative statements such as 62.2%, 1.7%, 32%, 95%, approximately 50%, and 46% are reported without the underlying numerators, denominators, uncertainty intervals, or, where applicable, explicit analysis units. The review itself emphasizes substantial inter-rater variability, including different definitions across epilepsy centers and possible confusion between versive and non-versive head turning. It also cautions that semiology may reflect ictal spread: different epileptogenic zones can activate the same symptomatogenic zone, and the same epileptogenic zone can activate different symptomatogenic zones. Finally, focal-appearing semiology can occur in generalized epilepsy, and the review reports conflicting signs within a single seizure; its proposed safeguards are standardization, unambiguous signs, observer consensus, sequence, and specificity.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The document is a narrative literature review organized by a semiological classification of paroxysmal events, auras, autonomic, dialeptic, motor, special, and additional lateralizing signs. It does not report a systematic search method, eligibility criteria, aggregate review population, cohort size, comparator, or common reference standard. Individual findings retain the population, phase, comparator, and cited-study attribution stated in the review.
sources.source_report_summary: This 2012 J Clin Neurol narrative review by Krikor Tufenkjian and Hans O. Lüders summarizes seizure-semiology findings considered useful for localizing the epileptogenic zone, with emphasis on prominent and consistent signs and on lateralizing signs. The review states that its information is based on literature review and results consistent with the authors' experience; it is not a report of one newly enrolled cohort.

sources.source_report_limitations: The article is a narrative critical appraisal rather than a single cohort or quantitative synthesis; most table entries are citation groupings without category counts, denominators, uncertainty intervals, or standardized analysis units. The source explicitly notes that impaired consciousness, short ictal duration, accompanying or evolving seizure types, and difficult ictal/postictal differentiation limit precise classification. The illustrated EEG panels are single case observations and do not establish cohort frequencies. Cited-study restatements above remain unverified against their cited targets because only this PDF and its fresh source package were in the evidence boundary. The body attributes one result to “Privitera and Kim [73]” and another to “Lösch et al. [74]”; this report preserves those source-native attributions without reconciling internal citation numbering against the bibliography. No sign identity is assigned.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The authors report an extensive literature search on the term “epileptic aphasia,” analysis of semiology and terminology indicating language-associated seizure symptoms, and an overview of EEG, etiology, brain imaging, and ictal language disorders. The document is not a single-cohort study; its evidence base includes cited case reports, case series, and studies involving ictal aphasia, aphasic status epilepticus (ASE), temporal/frontal/other focal epilepsies, and postictal language dysfunction. The review does not report one pooled analysis population or common denominator.
sources.source_report_summary: Unterberger et al. (Epilepsy & Behavior, 2021) is a narrative critical appraisal of epileptic aphasia and other ictal/postictal language disturbances. It reviews source terminology and semiology and summarizes EEG, etiology, brain imaging, and seizure-associated language lateralization/localization evidence. The article is relevant to language-associated seizure semiology, dominant-hemisphere lateralization, and the limits of finer localization.

findings.claim: The authors conclude that insulo-opercular epilepsy should be suspected in patients with somatosensory or neurovegetative symptoms, early focal tonic seizures involving the face and/or neck, and extensive perisylvian interictal or ictal discharges, and that SEEG is necessary in most suspected cases to define the epileptogenic zone.
findings.evidence_text: “Insulo-opercular epilepsy should be suspected” with the listed symptoms, early focal tonic signs, and extensive perisylvian discharges; “SEEG implantation is necessary to define the epileptogenic zone in most suspected” cases.
findings.laterality_localization: Extensive perisylvian scalp-discharge distribution and definition of the epileptogenic zone by SEEG; no additional side direction stated in the conclusion
findings.limitations: This is the authors’ synthesis from a retrospective, selected SEEG-defined cohort and is not presented as a prospectively validated diagnostic rule.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a retrospective, selected 22-patient series from a presurgical SEEG population; inclusion required complete presurgical evaluation and clear seizure-semiology video, and the cohort mixed pediatric and adult patients. Scalp-EEG interpretation used representative or predominant patterns, and at least two habitual seizures per patient were reviewed rather than every recorded seizure. The voxel-based PET comparison excluded five patients and used a left-transposed representation for right-sided epileptogenic foci; PET hypometabolism may extend beyond the seizure-onset or propagation cortex, as the authors note. Aggregate laterality is incomplete: several “ipsilateral” or “contralateral” descriptors do not restate their reference side, and many aggregate results do not provide side-specific counts. The online supporting information named on page 13 (Table S1 and Figure S1) is not included in the locked 13-page source package and was not reviewed.
sources.source_report_methods_population: The study retrospectively identified 22 consecutive medication-resistant patients evaluated between January 2015 and March 2018; 12 were adults and 10 were pediatric patients. Insulo-opercular seizure origin was defined by SEEG, and patients without complete presurgical evaluation or clear seizure-semiology video were excluded. At least two habitual seizures were reviewed per patient for scalp video-EEG (53 seizures total), and EI was computed for two habitual seizures per patient. PET visual/MRI-coregistration analyses involved the patient group; the voxel-based PET comparison used 17 patients after excluding three with previous epilepsy surgery and two younger than 7 years, compared with 18 healthy subjects.
sources.source_report_summary: Wang et al., “Electroclinical features of insulo-opercular epilepsy: an SEEG and PET study,” Annals of Clinical and Translational Neurology 2019;6:1165-1177, is an original retrospective empirical study of presurgical electroclinical features, interictal PET, and ictal SEEG in patients with SEEG-defined insulo-opercular epilepsy. Its in-scope contribution is a source-reported characterization of seizure semiology, scalp-EEG distribution, PET abnormalities, and EI-based localization.

findings.claim: Interictal EEG findings supported the movement-direction distinction: among patients with versive seizures, 22 had only a focus contralateral to the direction of head and eye movement, 5 had bilateral foci, and none had only an ipsilateral focus; among patients with nonversive seizures, 7 had bilateral foci, 2 only contralateral, and 1 only ipsilateral.
findings.evidence_text: Twenty-two of 27 patients with versive seizures had only contralateral interictal foci; none had only ipsilateral foci.
findings.laterality_localization: Interictal focus classified as bilateral, only contralateral, or only ipsilateral to the direction of head and eye movement; for versive seizures, a contralateral focus was concordant with the hemisphere of seizure onset
findings.limitations: Interictal focus is not the same measurement as ictal EEG seizure-onset location.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, paragraph beginning “The interictal EEG data supported these findings”

findings.population: 27 patients with versive seizures and 10 patients with nonversive seizures
findings.source_term: interictal EEG foci in versive and nonversive seizures

findings.claim: The ictal EEG pattern remained clearly lateralized into onset of the contraversive movement in 54 seizures from 24 patients; 3 previously lateralized seizures were obscured by EMG artifact, and 4 remaining seizures included 3 with nonlateralized EEG onset and 1 with temporal onset spreading equally to both temporal lobes before contraversion.
findings.evidence_text: The EEG seizure pattern remained clearly lateralized into the onset of the contraversive movement during 54 seizures from 24 patients.
findings.laterality_localization: In an illustrative seizure, ictal EEG began in the right mesial temporal lobe for 79 seconds, spread to both temporal lobes equally for 75 seconds, and was followed by leftward contraversion with left arm and face clonic activity; the movement remained contralateral to the initial onset hemisphere
findings.limitations: Three seizures with generalized EEG onset were interpreted using interictal focus in the methods, and EMG artifact obscured three previously lateralized patterns.
findings.locators: PDF p.2, paragraphs describing EEG lateralization and the bitemporal-spread seizure
findings.phase: Ictal EEG onset through contraversion; one seizure after spread to both temporal lobes
findings.population: 61 versive seizures from 27 patients
findings.source_term: EEG lateralization at onset of contraversive movement

findings.claim: Thirty-five of 61 versive seizures (57%) began with the versive movement; these were predominantly frontal-onset (91%) and none was temporal-onset, whereas the other versive seizures were preceded by quiet staring or staring with automatisms as detailed in Table 2.
findings.evidence_text: Thirty-five (57%) of the 61 versive seizures began with the versive movement.
findings.laterality_localization: Contraversive movement was related to the EEG-defined seizure-onset region; onset region was frontal, temporal, parietal, or occipital
findings.limitations: Quiet staring without automatisms occurred in both temporal and extratemporal onset seizures and was not assigned a specific mechanism.

findings.claim: Quiet staring preceded contraversion for 8 versive seizures for 2-31 seconds (mean 17), while staring with automatisms preceded contraversion for 18 seizures for 4-227 seconds (mean 34); all seizures with automatisms before contraversion originated in temporal lobes, whereas the quiet-staring subgroup arose from temporal (25%) and extratemporal (75%) locations.
findings.evidence_text: All seizures with contraversion preceded by automatisms originated in temporal lobes.
findings.laterality_localization: Contraversion followed a period of temporal localization when preceded by staring with automatisms; quiet-staring onset was temporal or extratemporal
findings.limitations: The paper did not report numerators for the 25% and 75% onset-region proportions in the quiet-staring subgroup.

findings.claim: During contraversion, arm and face motor activity occurred on the side toward which contraversion was directed: arm clonic movement or tonic posturing occurred in 32 of 61 versive seizures (52%), face tonic or clonic contraction in 26 of 55 seizures with continuously visible faces (47%), and arm and face involvement occurred with equal frequency in temporal and extratemporal onset seizures.
findings.evidence_text: During contraversion, 32 (52%) of versive seizures involved clonic arm movement or tonic posturing on the side of contraversion.
findings.laterality_localization: Arm and face activity occurred on the body side toward which contraversion was directed, described in the discussion as the contralateral arm and face
findings.limitations: Facial analysis excluded 6 seizures without continuous full facial visibility.

findings.claim: The authors interpret contraversion as primarily resulting from transcortical propagation of seizure discharge to frontal contraversive centers in the hemisphere of seizure onset, with the first versive movement clinically similar to movements elicited by electrical stimulation of Brodmann area 6 or 8; they note that contraversion occurred with frontal, temporal, parietal, and occipital onset seizures.
findings.evidence_text: Our findings suggested that version was primarily due to transcortical propagation of the seizure discharge to frontal contraversive centers.
findings.laterality_localization: Frontal contraversive fields anterior to the precentral gyrus; proposed propagation to frontal contraversive centers in the seizure-onset hemisphere; Brodmann areas 6 or 8 cited as stimulation analogues
findings.limitations: This is the authors’ mechanistic interpretation rather than a separately tested causal localization analysis; occipital evidence was one patient with two seizures.
findings.locators: PDF p.4, discussion of frontal contraversive fields and transcortical propagation; PDF p.4, paragraph on occipital onset; PDF p.5, conclusion
findings.phase: First versive movement during the seizure
findings.population: Current empirical series; onset regions represented in Table 1

findings.citation: Ochs R, Gloor P, Quesney F, Ives J, Olivier A, “Does head-turning during a seizure have lateralizing or localizing significance?” Neurology (Cleveland) 1984;34:884-90 [31]; Robillard A, Saint-Hilaire JM, Mercier M, Bouvier G, “The lateralizing and localizing value of adversion in epileptic seizures.” Neurology (Cleveland) 1983;33:1241-2 [32]
findings.claim: The current paper reports that Ochs et al. and Robillard et al. found ipsiversion in 50% and 48%, respectively, of seizures with head and eye turning and concluded that forced head turning at clinical seizure onset had no localizing or lateralizing value.
findings.evidence_text: Ochs et al. and Robillard et al. reported ipsiversion in 50% and 48% of seizures with head and eye turning.
findings.laterality_localization: Ipsiversive head/eye turning; cited authors’ conclusion was no localization or lateralization value
findings.limitations: Cited-study restatement only; the cited reports were not independently reviewed in this bounded review.
findings.locators: PDF p.3, discussion paragraph comparing Ochs and Robillard; PDF p.5, references 31-32
findings.phase: Head turning at clinical seizure onset
findings.population: Seizures with head and eye turning in the cited Ochs and Robillard reports; cohort details not reported here

sources.source_report_limitations: The cohort was selected for lateral head and eye movement and therefore does not represent all seizures. Two of 39 selected patients were excluded because EMG artifact obscured seizure onset. Three seizures had generalized ictal EEG onset and were assigned to an interictal focus; three other previously lateralized patterns were obscured by EMG artifact at contraversion. The distinction between versive and nonversive movement depended on high-quality video and consistent interpretation, and the authors note that lower-resolution or time-lapse recordings can mix subtle nonversive and forced movements. Ictal consciousness was difficult to assess because edited videotapes often lacked routine postictal interviews, so the authors could not reliably apply the contemporary partial-seizure consciousness distinction. Occipital-onset evidence comprised two seizures from one patient and was insufficient to evaluate mechanism. Background comparisons with cited studies are restatements from this paper and were not independently verified here. Page 6 is primarily references and page 7 is publisher information; no additional scientific findings were present in those pages.
sources.source_report_methods_population: Thirty-nine patients aged 1-48 years (mean 22) were selected for lateral head and eye movement during seizures; 2 were excluded because electromyographic artifact obscured electroencephalographic seizure onset. The analyzed sample was 37 patients with 74 spontaneous seizures: 20 patients were studied for complex partial seizures with or without secondary generalization and 17 for partial motor seizures with or without altered consciousness or secondary generalization. All seizures occurred spontaneously in the EEG laboratory, were recorded from onset, and had high-quality synchronized audio-video and EEG recordings; scalp, nasopharyngeal or sphenoidal electrodes were used, and 8 patients also had chronic subdural electrode arrays. Video and EEG were analyzed independently, and movement classification was performed without knowledge of EEG or clinical data. Ictal EEG seizure-onset location was used for all seizures except 3 with generalized ictal EEG onset, which were assigned to the location of the interictal focus because of other lateralizing EEG data. Table 1 onset totals were frontal 39 (12 patients), temporal 31 (22), parietal 2 (2), and occipital 2 (1); table values are seizures with patient counts in parentheses.
sources.source_report_summary: Original empirical observational study by Wyllie, Luders, Morris, Lesser, and Dinner, published in Neurology in 1986, evaluating whether forced lateral head and eye turning during spontaneous epileptic seizures lateralizes seizure onset. Independent blinded video and EEG review was used to compare versive and nonversive movements, onset region, preceding ictal behavior, associated motor signs, and secondary generalization.

sources.source_report_limitations: This is a two-case report without controls, a population denominator for the eye-deviation sign, or a statistical estimate of frequency, sensitivity, specificity, or predictive value. Case-1 has an unresolved internal laterality discrepancy: the case narrative and Fig. 1 describe right forced eye deviation, while the Fig. 5 caption labels the initial eyes as left version. The source presents MST involvement as an anatomical interpretation and hypothesis, not as a controlled causal demonstration. Cited-study statements are retained as unverified cited restatements and were not checked against the cited papers. No pages were unreadable or blocked; page 10 contained publication metadata and bibliography and contributed no additional source-native finding.
sources.source_report_methods_population: This is a two-case report with no control or comparator group. Case-1 was a 24-year-old right-handed man; 32 habitual seizures were recorded during 3 days of scalp video-EEG, with two followed by secondary GTCS, and two right-hemisphere SEEG implantations were performed 4 months apart. Case-2 was a 19-year-old right-handed man; three habitual seizures were captured on video-EEG and right temporal neocortical, temporal-pole, and medial-structure regions were explored with SEEG. The source describes scalp EEG, MRI, FDG-PET, SEEG onset and propagation, anatomical reconstruction, cortical resection, and seizure-free follow-up of 17 months for Case-1 and 25 months for Case-2. Case-1 MRI/FDG-PET was reported unremarkable for an evaluable lesion; Case-2 MRI and PET findings were reported in the right middle-posterior inferior temporal/fusiform and medial temporal regions. No cohort-wide denominator for ipsiversive eye deviation, no control comparison, and no population-level frequency or diagnostic statistic are reported.
sources.source_report_summary: Zhang et al., “Ipsiversive ictal eye deviation in inferioposterior temporal lobe epilepsy—Two SEEG cases report,” is a 2017 BMC Neurology case report describing two patients with focal seizures and initial ipsiversive eye deviation. The report uses scalp video-EEG, MRI/FDG-PET, ictal and interictal SEEG, electrode localization, and postoperative follow-up to relate the semiology to right inferioposterior/posterior temporal epileptogenic regions and the human MT/MST complex. It is relevant to sign-level semiology, localization, and laterality, but it is not a prevalence or diagnostic-accuracy study.
